A '''European Study Group with Industry (ESGI)''' is usually a [[week]]-long meeting where applied [[mathematician]]s work on problems presented by industry and research centres. The aim of the meeting is to solve or at least make progress on the problems.

The study group concept originated in [[Oxford]], in 1968 (initiated by [[Leslie Fox]] and [[Alan B Tayler|Alan Tayler]]). Subsequently, the format was adopted in other [[European countries]] to form ESGIs. Currently, with a variety of names, they appear in the same or a similar format throughout the world. More specific topics have also formed the subject of focussed meetings, such as the environment, medicine and agriculture.

Problems successfully tackled at study groups are discussed in a number of [[textbook]]s as well as a collection of case studies, European Success Stories in Industrial Mathematics. A guide for organising and running study groups is provided by the [[:fr:European Consortium for Mathematics in Industry|European Consortium for Mathematics in Industry]].

== European Study Group with Industry ==

A European Study Group with Industry or ESGI is a type of workshop where mathematicians work on problems presented by industry representatives. The meetings typically last five days, from Monday to Friday. On the Monday morning the industry representatives present problems of current interest to an audience of applied mathematicians. Subsequently, the mathematicians split into working groups to investigate the suggested topics. On the Friday solutions and results are presented back to the industry representative. After the meeting a report is prepared for the company, detailing the progress made and usually with suggestions for further work or experiments.

== History ==

The original Study Groups with Industry started in Oxford in 1968. The format provided a method for initiating interaction between universities and private industry which often led to further collaboration, student projects and new fields of research (many advances in the field of free or moving boundary problems are attributed to the industrial case studies of the 1970s.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Elliott|first1=C.M.|last2=Ockendon|first2=J.R.|title=Weak and variational methods for free and moving boundary problems|date=1982|publisher=Pitman Publishing|isbn=978-0-273-08503-4}}</ref>). Study groups were later adopted in other countries, starting in Europe and then spreading throughout the world. The subject areas have also diversified, for example the Mathematics in [[Medical education|Medicine Study]] Groups,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.maths-in-medicine.org/|title=Mathematics in Medicine Study Groups|website=Mathematics in Medicine Study Groups|accessdate=June 2, 2017}}</ref> Mathematics in the [[Botany|Plant Sciences]] Study Groups,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cpib.ac.uk/outreach/mpssg/|title=Mathematics in the Plant Sciences Study Group|access-date=June 2, 2017}}</ref> the environment, uncertainty quantification and [[agriculture]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths-in-industry.org/past/|title=Mathematics in Industry {{!}} Past Study Groups|last=Bentahar|first=K.|website=www.maths-in-industry.org|access-date=2018-06-05}}</ref>

The academics work on the problems for free. The following have been given as motivation for this work:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wits.ac.za/conferences/misgsa2016/|title=South African Maths in Industry Study Group|access-date=June 2, 2017}}</ref>

# Discovering new problems and research areas with practical applications.
# The possibility of further projects and collaboration with industry.
# The opportunity for future funding.

A number of reasons have also been quoted for companies to attend ESGIs:<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://miis.maths.ox.ac.uk/how/|title=Maths in Industry Information Service, How|access-date=June 2, 2017}}</ref>

# The possibility of a quick solution to their problem, or at least guidance on a way forward.
# Mathematicians can help to identify and correctly formulate a problem for further study.
# Access to state-of-the-art techniques.
# Building contacts with top researchers in a given field.

ESGIs are currently an activity of the European Consortium for Mathematics in Industry.<ref>{{cite web|last1=ECMI|title=European Consortium for Mathematics in Industry|url=https://ecmiindmath.org/|website=European Consortium for Mathematics in Industry|accessdate=22 February 2017}}</ref> Their ESGI webpage <ref>{{cite web|last1=ECMI ESGI|title=Study Groups|url=https://ecmiindmath.org/study-groups/|website=Study Groups|accessdate=22 February 2017}}</ref> contains details of European meetings and contact details for prospective industry or academics participants. The current co-ordinator of the ESGIs is Prof. Tim Myers of the [[Centre de Recerca Matemàtica|Centre de Recerca Matemática]], Barcelona.<ref>{{cite web|title=Centre de Recerca Matemática|url=http://www.crm.cat|website=CRM|accessdate=28 February 2017}}</ref> Between 2015 and 2019 ESGIs are eligible for funding through the COST network MI-Net (Maths for Industry Network).<ref>{{cite web|title=Mathematics for Industry Network|url=https://mi-network.org/|website=MI-Net|accessdate=28 February 2017}}</ref>

== International study groups ==

As well as being held throughout Europe, annual study groups take place in [[Australia]],<ref>{{cite web|title=MISG|url=http://mathsinindustry.com/|website=Mathematics in Industry Study Group|accessdate=28 February 2017}}</ref> [[Brazil]], [[Canada]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Industrial Problem Solving Workshops|url=https://www.pims.math.ca/industrial/industrial-workshops|website=Industrial Workshops|accessdate=28 February 2017}}</ref> [[India]], [[New Zealand]],<ref>{{cite web|title=MINZ|url=http://www.minz.org.nz/|website=Mathematics in Industry New Zealand|accessdate=28 February 2017}}</ref> [[United States]], [[Russia]], and [[South Africa]]. A site dedicated solely to [[Netherlands|Dutch]] study groups may be found here [https://www.swi-wiskunde.nl/editions/ Dutch ESGI]. Information on past and upcoming meetings throughout the world may be found on the Mathematics in Industry Information Service website.<ref>{{cite web|last1=MIIS|title=Mathematics in Industry Information Service|url=http://miis.maths.ox.ac.uk/|accessdate=22 February 2017}}</ref>

== Literature ==

There are many books on mathematical modelling, a number of them containing problems arising from ESGIs or other study groups from around the world, examples include:
# ''Practical Applied Mathematics Modelling, Analysis, Approximation''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Howison|first1=S.D.|title=Practical Applied Mathematics Modelling, Analysis, Approximation|date=2005|publisher=Cambridge Texts in Applied Mathematics}}</ref>
# ''Topics in Industrial Mathematics: Case Studies and Related Mathematical Methods''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Neunzert|first1=H.|last2=Siddiqi|first2=A.H.|title=Topics in Industrial Mathematics: Case Studies and Related Mathematical Methods|date=2000|publisher=Springer}}</ref>
# ''Industrial Mathematics: A Course in Solving Real-World Problems''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Friedman|first1=A|last2=Littman|first2=W|title=Industrial Mathematics: A Course in Solving Real-World Problems|date=1994|publisher=SIAM|doi=10.1137/1.9781611971545|isbn=978-0-89871-324-4}}</ref>

The book ''European Success Stories in Industrial Mathematics''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lery|display-authors=etal|title=European Success Stories in Industrial Mathematics|date=2012|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-642-23847-5}}</ref> contains brief descriptions of a wide variety of industrial mathematics case studies. The Mathematics in Industry Information Service contains a large repository of past reports from study groups throughout the  world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths-in-industry.org/past/|title=MIIS Past Reports|access-date=June 2, 2017}}</ref>

A guide for organising and running study groups, the ESGI Handbook,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://mi-network.org/resources/handbook-for-running-a-sustainable-european-study-groups-with-industry/|title=ESGI Handbook|date=2018-04-17|work=MI-NET|access-date=2018-06-05|language=en-US}}</ref> has been developed by the Mathematics for Industry Network.
